claim: Mice trained to perform progressively faster sequences of lever presses to obtain reinforcement reduced variability in sequence frequency.
source: Animals trained to perform progressively faster sequences of lever presses to obtain reinforcement reduced variability in sequence frequency, but increased variability in an orthogonal feature (sequence duration).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing decrease in frequency variability across training sessions (Figure 2C,E)

claim: Mice trained to perform progressively faster sequences of lever presses increased variability in sequence duration.
source: Animals trained to perform progressively faster sequences of lever presses to obtain reinforcement reduced variability in sequence frequency, but increased variability in an orthogonal feature (sequence duration).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing increase in duration variability across training sessions (Figure 2D,F)

claim: Trial-to-trial variability of the activity of motor cortex and striatal projection neurons was higher early in training.
source: Trial-to-trial variability of the activity of motor cortex and striatal projection neurons was higher early in training and subsequently decreased with learning, without changes in average firing rate.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing higher Fano factor in early sessions (Figure 4A)

claim: Trial-to-trial variability of the activity of motor cortex and striatal projection neurons subsequently decreased with learning.
source: Trial-to-trial variability of the activity of motor cortex and striatal projection neurons was higher early in training and subsequently decreased with learning, without changes in average firing rate.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing decreased Fano factor across training (Figure 4A)

claim: Average firing rate of motor cortex and striatal projection neurons did not change with learning.
source: Trial-to-trial variability of the activity of motor cortex and striatal projection neurons was higher early in training and subsequently decreased with learning, without changes in average firing rate.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing no significant changes in firing rate across sessions (Figure 4E-H)

claim: As training progressed, variability in corticostriatal activity became progressively more correlated with behavioral variability in frequency.
source: As training progressed, variability in corticostriatal activity became progressively more correlated with behavioral variability, but specifically with variability in frequency.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing increasing correlation between neural and frequency variability (Figure 6C)

claim: Variability in corticostriatal activity did not become correlated with variability in sequence duration.
source: As training progressed, variability in corticostriatal activity became progressively more correlated with behavioral variability, but specifically with variability in frequency.
evidence: Inferred from the specific correlation with frequency but not duration (Figure 6D)

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity was required for the reduction in frequency variability.
source: Corticostriatal plasticity was required for the reduction in frequency variability, but not for variability in sequence duration.
evidence: Supported by mutant mouse experiments showing impaired frequency variability reduction in SPN NR1-KO mice (Figure 7F)

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity was not required for changes in variability in sequence duration.
source: Corticostriatal plasticity was required for the reduction in frequency variability, but not for variability in sequence duration.
evidence: Supported by mutant mouse experiments showing no difference in duration variability modulation between groups (Figure 7G)

claim: During motor learning corticostriatal dynamics encode the refinement of specific behavioral features that change the probability of obtaining outcomes.
source: These data suggest that during motor learning corticostriatal dynamics encode the refinement of specific behavioral features that change the probability of obtaining outcomes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from combined behavioral, electrophysiological, and genetic manipulation data

claim: Acquiring novel skills requires exploration of the behavioral space, which is critical for learning.
source: Acquiring novel skills usually requires exploration of the behavioral space, which is critical for learning (Skinner, 1981; Sutton and Barto, 1998; Grunow and Neuringer, 2002; Kao et al., 2005; Olveczky et al., 2005; Tumer and Brainard, 2007; Miller et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Acquiring novel skills requires the selection of the appropriate behavioral features that lead to the desired outcomes.
source: It also requires the selection of the appropriate behavioral features that lead to the desired outcomes (Skinner, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The motor system can learn complex movements by optimizing motor variability in task-relevant dimensions.
source: It has been postulated that the motor system can learn complex movements by optimizing motor variability in task-relevant dimensions, correcting only deviations that interfere with the final output of the action (Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Scott, 2004; Valero-Cuevas et al., 2009; Diedrichsen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical work

claim: Humans can perform smooth movements even in the presence of noise by optimizing the precision of an action endpoint.
source: By optimizing the precision of an action endpoint, for example, humans can perform smooth movements even in the presence of noise (Harris and Wolpert, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior empirical work

claim: Selecting task-relevant features and decreasing task-relevant variability might be a critical component of motor learning.
source: Selecting task-relevant features and decreasing task-relevant variability might therefore be a critical component of motor learning (Franklin and Wolpert, 2008; Cohen and Sternad, 2009; Valero-Cuevas et al., 2009; Costa, 2011; Shmuelof et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Cortical and basal ganglia circuits are important for the selection of task-relevant features.
source: It has been suggested that cortical and basal ganglia circuits are important for the selection of task-relevant features (Costa et al., 2004; Barnes et al., 2005; Kao et al., 2005; Olveczky et al., 2005; Jin and Costa, 2010; Woolley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: The initial stages of learning have increased behavioral variability.
source: Consistently, it has been previously shown that the initial stages of learning have increased behavioral (Tumer and Brainard, 2007; Jin and Costa, 2010; Miller et al., 2010) and neuronal (Costa et al., 2004; Barnes et al., 2005) variability, but as specific movements are consolidated, neural variability is reduced in these circuits (Costa et al., 2004; Kao et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior empirical work

claim: The initial stages of learning have increased neuronal variability.
source: Consistently, it has been previously shown that the initial stages of learning have increased behavioral (Tumer and Brainard, 2007; Jin and Costa, 2010; Miller et al., 2010) and neuronal (Costa et al., 2004; Barnes et al., 2005) variability, but as specific movements are consolidated, neural variability is reduced in these circuits (Costa et al., 2004; Kao et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior empirical work

claim: As specific movements are consolidated, neural variability is reduced in cortical and basal ganglia circuits.
source: Consistently, it has been previously shown that the initial stages of learning have increased behavioral (Tumer and Brainard, 2007; Jin and Costa, 2010; Miller et al., 2010) and neuronal (Costa et al., 2004; Barnes et al., 2005) variability, but as specific movements are consolidated, neural variability is reduced in these circuits (Costa et al., 2004; Kao et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior empirical work

claim: After initial motor and neural exploration, specific patterns are selected and consolidated.
source: This suggests that after initial motor and neural exploration, specific patterns are selected and consolidated (Costa, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior theoretical work

claim: The total number of lever presses per minute increased throughout training.
source: The total number of lever presses per minute increased throughout training (F8,152 = 41.34, p < 0.0001; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing increase in press rate

claim: Animals rapidly started to organize their behavior in self-paced bouts or sequences of lever presses.
source: animals rapidly started to organize their behavior in self-paced bouts or sequences of lever presses, until there were almost no single presses (Figure 1C,E and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data and video showing sequence organization

claim: The percentage of lever presses performed within a sequence increased significantly from 56.98 ± 3.98 in the first session to 98.26 ± 0.53 in the last training session.
source: The percentage of lever presses performed within a sequence increased significantly from 56.98 ± 3.98 in the first session of covert target introduction, to 98.26 ± 0.53 in the last training session (F8,152 = 60.22, p < 0.0001; Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing increase in sequence organization

claim: The number of sequences performed per minute increased with training.
source: the number of sequences performed per minute increased with training (F8,152 = 32.23, p < 0.0001; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing increase in sequence rate

claim: The distance of consecutive IPIs to the final target frequency decreased consistently with training.
source: Importantly, with training, the distance of consecutive IPIs (summed in bins of 3 IPIs to mimic the online criteria) to the final target frequency (3 IPIs <660 ms, ∼4.5 Hz) decreased consistently (F8,152 = 25.76, p < 0.0001; Figure 1F)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing decreased distance to target

claim: The spread around the target frequency decreased with training.
source: Not only did the distance to the end target decrease, but the spread around the target also decreased (F8,152 = 9.616, p < 0.001; calculated as the standard deviation around the target frequency, Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing decreased spread

claim: Animals gradually increased the percentage of press bouts that would achieve the minimum target frequency of the last session.
source: Consistently, animals gradually increased the percentage of press bouts that would achieve the minimum target frequency of the last session (end-target: 3 IPIs <660 ms, ∼4.5 Hz; F8,152 = 14.15, p < 0.0001; Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing increased target achievement

claim: Animals learned to shape their behavior to get closer to the covert target.
source: These data indicate that animals learned to shape their behavior to get closer to the covert target.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple behavioral measures showing approach to target

claim: The mean frequency of each pressing bout decreased slightly with training.
source: The mean frequency of each pressing bout (sequence frequency) decreased slightly (F8,152 = 2.372, p = 0.0195, Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing slight decrease in mean frequency

claim: The duration of each pressing bout increased with training.
source: while the duration of each pressing bout (sequence duration) increased with training (F8,152 = 22.69, p < 0.0001, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing increase in sequence duration

claim: The variance of sequence frequency decreased significantly throughout training.
source: While the variability of sequence frequency decreased significantly throughout training (variance: F8,152 = 4.450, p < 0.0001, Figure 2C; Fano factor: F8,152 = 5.343, p < 0.0001, Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figures showing decreased frequency variability

claim: The variability of sequence duration significantly increased with training.
source: the variability of sequence duration significantly increased (variance: F8,152 = 11.15, p < 0.0001, Figure 2D; Fano factor: F8,152 = 16.86, p < 0.0001, Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figures showing increased duration variability

claim: The sequence-to-sequence variability of sequence frequency and sequence duration was independent.
source: The sequence-to-sequence variability of these two behavioral features was independent as there was no correlation between the variability in sequence frequency and the variability in sequence duration (variance: R2 = 0.0135; Fano factor: R2 = 0.0119, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing lack of relationship between frequency and duration variability

claim: There is a strong correlation between variability in sequence duration and variability in sequence length.
source: This is in contrast with a strong correlation observed between variability in sequence duration and the variability in sequence length—number of presses (variance: R2 = 0.8710; Fano factor: R2 = 0.8839, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing strong relationship between duration and length variability

claim: In the control task, the variability of sequence frequency did not decrease with training.
source: in this control task the variability of sequence frequency did not decrease with training (F8,56 = 1.049, p = 0.4113)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of control task data

claim: In the control task, variability in sequence duration decreased with training.
source: while variability in sequence duration did (F8,56 = 4.589, p = 0.0002) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure of control task data

claim: The decrease in variability in sequence frequency was task-specific.
source: These data indicate that the decrease in variability in sequence frequency was task-specific.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison between frequency task and control task

claim: Sequences leading to reinforcement had significantly lower variability in frequency compared to non-reinforced sequences.
source: We verified that sequences leading to reinforcement had indeed significantly lower variability in frequency compared to non-reinforced sequences (main effect of reinforcement, F1,38 = 7.608, p = 0.0089, Figure 3C and F1,38 = 28.34, p < 0.0001, Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figures comparing reinforced vs non-reinforced sequences

claim: There were no significant differences in the variability of sequence duration between reinforced and non-reinforced sequences.
source: but there were no significant differences in the variability of sequence duration between reinforced and non-reinforced sequences (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: Supported by figures showing no difference in duration variability between reinforced and non-reinforced sequences

claim: Mice selectively reduced variability in the behavioral domains where variability affected the probability of reinforcement.
source: These results suggest that mice selectively reduced variability in the behavioral domains where variability affected the probability of reinforcement (sequence frequency), but not in domains where variability did not change this probability (sequence duration).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of reinforced vs non-reinforced sequences

claim: An average of 18 M1 units and 10 DS units were simultaneously recorded per animal, per session.
source: In order to investigate the dynamics of cortical and striatal circuits during the acquisition and performance of the fast lever pressing task, we continuously recorded extracellular neuronal activity simultaneously in layer 5 of the primary motor cortex (M1), and in the dorsal striatum (DS) of mice during the full duration of training (4 days, N = 7 animals, average of 18 M1 units and 10 DS units simultaneously recorded per animal, per session).
evidence: Description of experimental methods and data collection

claim: 49 M1 units and 21 DS units were tracked as stable cells throughout the whole period of training.
source: Non-stop continuous electrophysiological recordings across 4 days encompassing all the sessions of training allowed us to track the activity of a subset of 'stable' cells throughout the whole period of training (49 M1 units, 21 DS Units).
evidence: Description of stable cell tracking methodology and results

claim: Sequence-to-sequence variability in the activity of individual neurons in DS decreased with training.
source: We found a high sequence-to-sequence variability in the activity of individual neurons (measured by the Fano factor of the firing rate) in the first couple of sessions, that then decreased with training (DS: F8,48 = 2.767, p < 0.05; M1: F8,48 = 2.771, p < 0.05; Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing decreased neural variability

claim: Sequence-to-sequence variability in the activity of individual neurons in M1 decreased with training.
source: We found a high sequence-to-sequence variability in the activity of individual neurons (measured by the Fano factor of the firing rate) in the first couple of sessions, that then decreased with training (DS: F8,48 = 2.767, p < 0.05; M1: F8,48 = 2.771, p < 0.05; Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing decreased neural variability

claim: Dynamics in neuronal variability were observed during the performance of lever-press sequences, but not during baseline periods.
source: These dynamics in neuronal variability were observed during the performance of lever-press sequences, but not during baseline periods (measured from 5 to 2 s before the initiation of each sequence), when the animals were not actively engaged in lever pressing (DS: F8,48 = 1.117, p = 0.3324; M1: F8,48 = 1.459, p = 0.1973; Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure comparing sequence vs baseline variability

claim: The decrease in neuronal variability was observed when using exclusively stable cells for analysis.
source: The decrease in neuronal variability was also observed when using exclusively 'stable' cells for this analysis (DS: F8,160 = 5.223, p < 0.0001; M1 F8,384 = 12.72, p < 0.0001; Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure of stable cell data

claim: The differences in variability throughout learning could be observed in individual cells and did not represent a shift in the population of neurons recorded across days.
source: showing that the differences in variability throughout learning could be observed in individual cells, and did not represent a shift in the population of neurons recorded across days.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from stable cell analysis

claim: The average firing rate of individual cells did not change significantly across sessions or across days.
source: Importantly, the average firing rate of individual cells did not change significantly, neither across sessions nor across days (p > 0.05 for all conditions, Figure 4E–H)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figures showing stable firing rates

claim: The reduction in variability was not attributable to overall changes in firing rate, but instead to the selection/refinement of particular firing patterns related to sequence execution.
source: suggesting that the reduction in variability was not attributable to overall changes in firing rate, but instead to the selection/refinement of a particular firing patterns related to sequence execution.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from dissociation between variability and firing rate changes

claim: Individual stable cells showed higher variability relative to baseline during the initial sessions.
source: Further analysis of these dynamics for individual stable cells clearly showed higher variability relative to baseline during the initial sessions (first session DS: W = 134, p = 0.0107; first session M1: W = 1119, p < 0.0001)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of individual cell data

claim: Individual stable cells reached the same levels of variability as baseline at the end of training.
source: that decreased throughout training until it reached the same levels of baseline at the end of training (last session DS: W = 73, p = 0.2157; last session M1: W = 253, p = 0.2121; Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure of individual cell data

claim: Average firing rates did not show any significant modulation in relation to baseline throughout the whole period of training.
source: Again, average firing rates did not show any significant modulation in relation to baseline throughout the whole period of training (DS: F8,160 = 1.031, p = 0.4153; M1: F8,384 = 1.757, p = 0.084; Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing stable firing rate modulation

claim: Neuronal variability was still elevated in early sessions and decreased as training progressed when analyzing sequences matched for frequency and duration.
source: We observed that neuronal variability was still elevated in early sessions and decreased as training progressed (DS: F8,48 = 2.732, p = 0.0144; M1: F8,48 = 2.491, p = 0.0239; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure of matched sequence data

claim: The decrease in neural variability was not due to gross changes in behavior.
source: This decrease in sequence-to-sequence variability of neural activity did not seem to result from the behavior becoming more stereotyped with training, as variability in behavior decreased for frequency but increased for duration (Figure 2). To further control that the decrease in neural variability was due to gross changes in behavior we restricted our analyses to sequences matched for frequency (t48 = 1.800, p = 0.0781) and duration (t48 = 1.733, p = 0.0895) between early and late sessions (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by matched sequence analysis controlling for behavioral changes

claim: The decrease in corticostriatal variability is not related to a general decrease in behavioral variability.
source: The results above suggest that the decrease in corticostriatal variability is not related to a general decrease in behavioral variability.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from dissociation between neural and behavioral variability patterns

claim: There was a significant increase in correlation between neuronal and behavior variability specific for sequence frequency.
source: Analyses of the relationship between the variability of the recorded units and the variability of each independent behavior feature revealed a significant increase in correlation between neuronal and behavior variability, specific for sequence frequency (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and figure showing increased correlation with frequency

claim: There was no significant increase in correlation between neuronal and behavior variability for sequence duration.
source: Analyses of the relationship between the variability of the recorded units and the variability of each independent behavior feature revealed a significant increase in correlation between neuronal and behavior variability, specific for sequence frequency (Figure 6C), but not for duration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and figure showing no correlation with duration

claim: The decrease in variability in M1 and DS is not just a reflection of a more constrained performance of the movement as training progresses.
source: These results show that the decrease in variability in M1 and DS is not just a reflection of a more constrained performance of the movement as training progresses; variability of the movement decreased in a specific dimension but it increased in others were no significant correlation with neuronal variability was evident.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from differential correlations with different behavioral dimensions

claim: No significant correlations were observed between the firing rate of neurons and the variability of any of the behavior features.
source: Furthermore, no significant correlations were observed between the firing rate of neurons and the variability any of the behavior features (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing no relationship between firing rate and behavioral variability

claim: The observed relationship between neuronal and behavior dynamics was not the reflex of a general increase in correlation between neuronal activity and behavior.
source: indicating again that the observed relationship between neuronal and behavior dynamics was not the reflex of a general increase in correlation between neuronal activity and behavior.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from lack of correlation between firing rate and behavioral variability

claim: At the onset of training the sequence-to-sequence variability of neural activity in DS and M1 in each animal was not correlated.
source: We verified that at the onset of training the sequence-to-sequence variability of neural activity in DS and M1 in each animal was not correlated.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of early training data

claim: A strong correlation between the variability in DS and M1 rapidly emerged during training.
source: However, a strong correlation between the variability in DS and M1 rapidly emerged during training (p < 0.05 for all except the first training session, Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and figure showing emergence of M1-DS correlation

claim: As behavioral variability is refined, neural variability in M1 and striatum becomes correlated.
source: suggesting that as behavioral variability is refined, neural variability in M1 and striatum becomes correlated.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from emergence of M1-DS correlation during training

claim: Mutant animals with NMDA receptors deleted specifically at glutamatergic synapses of striatal projection neurons have impaired corticostriatal plasticity.
source: We decided to directly test if the observed reduction in sequence frequency variability is dependent on corticostriatal plasticity by using mutant mice with NMDA receptors deleted specifically at glutamatergic synapses of striatal projection neurons (RGS9-LCre::Grin1tm1Yql; referred to in the figures as striatal projection neuron SPN NR1-KO), which have impaired corticostriatal plasticity (Dang et al., 2006), and control littermates.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work characterizing the mutant

claim: The distance to target decreased in littermate controls with training.
source: As expected, the distance to target (Controls: p = 0.0450, t5 = 2.657, Figure 7B) and spread around the target (Controls: p = 0.0179, t5 = 3.466, Figure 7C) decreased in littermate controls.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure of control animal data

claim: The spread around the target decreased in littermate controls with training.
source: As expected, the distance to target (Controls: p = 0.0450, t5 = 2.657, Figure 7B) and spread around the target (Controls: p = 0.0179, t5 = 3.466, Figure 7C) decreased in littermate controls.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure of control animal data

claim: Neither distance to target nor spread around the target changed with training in mutants.
source: However, neither of these measures changed with training in mutants (Mutants: p = 0.3535, t6 = 1.005; and p = 0.2817, t6 = 1.183, respectively; Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure of mutant animal data

claim: RGS9-LCre::Grin1tm1Yql mutants did not decrease sequence frequency variability during training, in contrast to littermate controls which did.
source: However, planned comparisons did show that RGS9-LCre::Grin1tm1Yql mutants did not decrease sequence frequency variability during training, in contrast to littermate controls which did (significant main effect of training time: F1,10 = 10.13, p = 0.009; Posthocs: Mutant group: t10 = 1.38, p = 0.1964; Control group: t10 = 3.00, p = 0.0134).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing mutant and control groups

claim: No differences in the modulation of sequence duration variability were observed between mutant and control groups.
source: Importantly, no differences in the modulation of sequence duration variability were observed between the two groups (no significant main effect for genotype: Duration FF: F1,10 = 0.02, p = 0.887) (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure comparing mutant and control groups

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity is required for the reduction in variability of specific behavioral features that change the probability of reinforcement.
source: These data suggest that corticostriatal plasticity is required for the reduction in variability of specific behavioral features that change the probability of reinforcement.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mutant mouse experiments showing selective impairment

claim: Both sequence frequency and duration would be classically considered task-relevant.
source: These results are interesting because both features would be classically considered task-relevant—a covert sequence of four presses, which is the minimum to produce a reinforcer in this task, has to have a minimal duration.
evidence: Logical inference about task structure

claim: Only changes in frequency variability were differentially reinforced.
source: However, although both features could be considered relevant for the task, only changes in frequency variability were differentially reinforced.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis of reinforcement contingencies

claim: Animals reduced frequency variability because that was what was reinforced throughout training.
source: Thus, our results indicate that animals reduced frequency variability because that was what was reinforced throughout training.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from reinforcement analysis and control task comparison

claim: The results are in line with data demonstrating differential modulation of the different components of task space during learning.
source: This in line with data demonstrating differential modulation of the different components of task space during learning (Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Müller and Sternad, 2004; Cohen and Sternad, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: In previous studies where animals performed operant tasks where the constrains were more relaxed, animals decreased variability in all behavioral domains.
source: In previous studies from our group where animals performed operant tasks where the constrains were more relaxed (Jin and Costa, 2010), animals decreased variability in all behavioral domains (i.e., they became more stereotypical overall).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work from the same group

claim: When faced with a more challenging task, animals decreased variability in the domain that was critical for getting a reinforcer, but increased variability in orthogonal domains.
source: However, when faced with a more challenging task as in the present study, they decreased variability in the domain that was critical for getting a reinforcer, but increased variability in orthogonal domains (i.e., they were more stereotypical in just a particular domain).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from current study results

claim: The increase in variability in the orthogonal behavioral domains might happen because in difficult tasks animals try to minimize the effort to obtain reinforcers.
source: It could be that the increase in variability in the orthogonal behavioral domains happens because in difficult tasks animals try to minimize the effort to obtain reinforcers, and hence do not attempt to reduce variability in more than one independent domain.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed results

claim: Mice might have increased the duration of the sequence as a strategy to try to increase the probability of getting a successful covert pattern in that sequence.
source: Alternatively, it could also be that mice increased the duration of the sequence (and the correlated number of presses) as a strategy to try to increase the probability of getting a successful covert pattern in that sequence.
evidence: Alternative speculative explanation for observed results

claim: The second possibility (that mice increased duration as a strategy) is less likely, given that the two behavioral features were not correlated, and that sequences of different durations were equally likely to get reinforced.
source: However, this second possibility is less likely, given that the two behavioral features were not correlated, and that sequences of different durations were equally likely to get reinforced.
evidence: Inference based on data showing independence of features

claim: In more challenging motor tasks it is difficult to reduce variability in all domains, and animals seem to differentially refine the motor patterns that led to reinforcement.
source: These data suggest that in more challenging motor tasks it is difficult to reduce variability in all domains, and animals seem to differentially refine the motor patterns that led to reinforcement.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of current and prior studies

claim: The number of sequences that comply with the minimum frequency required for the last session increased with training.
source: Consistently, the number of sequences that comply with the minimum frequency required for the last session (end-target) increased with training and the distance to the end-target decreased with training, indicating that mice implicitly learned to shape their behavior to match the task requirements.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing approach to target

claim: Mice implicitly learned to shape their behavior to match the task requirements.
source: Consistently, the number of sequences that comply with the minimum frequency required for the last session (end-target) increased with training and the distance to the end-target decreased with training, indicating that mice implicitly learned to shape their behavior to match the task requirements.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from behavioral shaping data

claim: Variability in the spike patterns of individual neurons and populations of neurons may be the bases for a process of behavioral exploration.
source: Variability in the spike patterns of individual neurons and populations of neurons may be the bases for a process of behavioral exploration (or trial) (Olveczky et al., 2005; Kao et al., 2005; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: A decrease in neural variability may reflect a process of selection of specific patterns of neural activity that lead to specific behavioral outputs.
source: while a decrease in neural variability may reflect a process of selection of specific patterns of neural activity that lead to specific behavioral outputs (Costa et al., 2004; Kao et al., 2005; Fee and Goldberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: A decrease in corticostriatal variability as a motor task is learned could correspond to the process of selection and consolidation of specific motor patterns.
source: It has been suggested that a decrease in corticostriatal variability as a motor task is learned (Costa et al., 2004; Barnes et al., 2005) could correspond to the process of selection and consolidation of specific motor patterns (Costa, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The decrease in neural variability in corticostriatal circuits correlates specifically with the decrease in variability of a particular behavior domain.
source: Here, we show that this decrease in neural variability in corticostriatal circuits correlates specifically with the decrease in variability of a particular behavior domain.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from correlation analysis in current study

claim: The neural patterns in motor cortex and sensorimotor striatum that give rise to the behavioral patterns that are reinforced are progressively selected.
source: These data suggest that the neural patterns in motor cortex and sensorimotor striatum that give rise to the behavioral patterns that are reinforced are progressively selected.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from correlation between neural and behavioral variability

claim: Changes in motor variability that are not specifically reinforced but are part of a strategy or driven by effort reduction may be encoded somewhere else.
source: Provocatively, it also suggests that changes in motor variability that are not specifically reinforced but are part of a strategy or driven by effort reduction may be encoded somewhere else.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of lack of correlation with duration variability

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity is important for the refinement of specific behavior features.
source: Finally, we also show that corticostriatal plasticity is important for the refinement of specific behavior features.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mutant mouse experiments

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity plays an important role in selecting the appropriate implicit neural and behavioral patterns that are reinforced.
source: Our data therefore suggests an important role for corticostriatal plasticity in selecting the appropriate implicit neural and behavioral patterns that are reinforced (Costa, 2011).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mutant mouse experiments with citation to prior theoretical work

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity did not seem to be necessary for the increase in behavioral variability in other domains.
source: However corticostriatal plasticity did not seem to be necessary for the increase in behavioral variability in other domains (Goldberg and Fee, 2011).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mutant mouse experiments showing no effect on duration variability

claim: Several studies have suggested that the basal ganglia, dopaminergic system, specific cortical circuits, or cerebellar circuits could subserve the function of generating variability.
source: Although in this study we don't investigate the mechanisms underlying the generation of variability, several studies have suggested that the basal ganglia, dopaminergic system, specific cortical circuits, or cerebellar circuits could subserve this function (Olveczky et al., 2005; Costa et al., 2006; Leblois et al., 2010; Costa, 2011; Fee and Goldberg, 2011; Shmuelof and Krakauer, 2011; Woolley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature
